title: Comparing, and what's going on right now
goal: Two final tools: **comparison** (bigger, cheapest) and **the -ing form** — which Brazil builds differently from Portugal.

dialogs.title: Dialogue — Rio ou São Paulo?
dialogs.intro: Brazil's eternal debate, staged at a cafeteria table.

notes: **Tá achando, tô gostando, estamos comendo — the -ing form appears several times in this dialogue.** In Brazil, this form is used even more than English "-ing", including for things going on over weeks: *Estou aprendendo português* ("I'm learning Portuguese" — not this very second, but these days).

⚠️ **In Portugal the sentence is *estou a aprender*.** That form is correct and understood in Brazil, but it instantly marks you as having learned from European sources. This module uses the Brazilian form: *estar* + a verb ending in **-ndo**.

**Maior do que and pior que** — two irregular comparatives. *Grande* doesn't become *mais grande* but **maior**; *ruim* doesn't become *mais ruim* but **pior** — just as English says "better", not "more good". There are only four words like this, and all are common.
**Duvido!** literally "I doubt it", means "no way!" or "I don't believe it!" — said jokingly. It's in the same family as *Sério?* and *Jura?* ("swear?").
**Aliás** means "by the way" or "in fact", and it's one of those linking words that make your conversation sound much more mature. Its casual equivalent: *por sinal*.

grammars.title: Comparison
body: Three formulas cover it all. Note that the adjective still agrees with its noun, as usual.

head: Pattern
Example
English
rows: *O Rio é mais bonito que São Paulo.*
Rio is prettier than São Paulo.
This one is less expensive than that one.
*A comida aqui é tão boa quanto lá.*
The food here is as good as there.
It's the biggest city in Brazil.
It's the cheapest in the shop.

after: **Do que and que are both correct.** *Mais bonito do que* and *mais bonito que* are interchangeable; the second is shorter and heard more often.

⚠️ To say "the most … in …", Portuguese uses **de**, not *em*: *a maior cidade **do** Brasil*, *o melhor restaurante **da** cidade*. English says "the biggest city **in** Brazil"; Portuguese says "of Brazil".

grammars.title: Four irregular comparisons
body: Four adjectives that refuse *mais*. All of them are common, so learn them now.
after: ⚠️ *Mais bom* and *mais grande* are mistakes people notice instantly. The right forms are *melhor* and *maior*, and they **don't change** for gender: *o melhor restaurante*, *a melhor comida*.
*Melhor* also means "better" in the advice sense from unit 18, and *pior* is also used as an exclamation: *Pior que é verdade* = "the worst part is, it's true".

grammars.title: The -ing form: estar + -ndo
body: Drop the infinitive ending and add **-ando**, **-endo** or **-indo**. There are no exceptions at all in the whole of Portuguese.
after: **Estou indo! is one of the most frequently texted phrases in Brazil** — it means "on my way". The clipped form, *tô indo*, is even more common.

**This form also works in the past**, with *estava*: *Eu estava dormindo quando você ligou* = "I was sleeping when you called". Notice that the background uses the *imperfeito* from unit 17 — two tools working together.
⚠️ Unlike English, this form is **not** used for the future. "I'm leaving tomorrow" isn't *estou indo amanhã* but *vou amanhã* or *vou viajar amanhã*.

blocks.text: A short, useful exercise: pick two cities you know, then write five comparison sentences about them using five pairs of adjectives from above.

sections.title: Tô, tá, e o resto: Brazilian clipped forms

blocks.text: You've already met some of these. Here's the full list in one place, because without it you'll struggle to follow fast conversation.

⚠️ These forms **aren't used in formal writing** — don't write *tô* in a job application. But they're perfectly normal in WhatsApp messages, social media and all spoken conversation, from students to professors.
*Cê* is the most extreme — it's hardly ever written, but very often said. If you hear something like "say vy?", that's *Você vai?*

items: When I was a kid → *Quando eu era criança*
I used to play in the street → *Eu brincava na rua*
The house was small → *A casa era pequena*
I miss it so much! → *Que saudade!*
I miss you → *Estou com saudade de você*

exercises.prompt: Complete the comparison. Write only the missing word.
items: O Rio é mais bonito ____ São Paulo.
Esse livro é ____ caro que aquele. (more)
A comida aqui é tão boa ____ lá.
O metrô é ____ rápido que o ônibus. (more)
Essa casa é ____ suja que a outra. (less)
